source: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Test-enhanced learning, Psychological Science, Exp 1
finding: Students read prose passages, then restudied or took one free-recall test (no feedback). Restudy won on a 5-min test but testing won after 2 days and 1 week. This crossover is the core testing-effect result.
numbers: N=120 undergraduates, 40 per final-test delay. 5 min: restudy 81% vs test 75% idea units (d=0.52). 2 days: test 68% vs restudy 54% (d=0.95). 1 week: test 56% vs restudy 42% (d=0.83). Interaction F(2,117)=32.10, partial eta2=.35. Tested group at 1 week matched the restudy group at 2 days.
limits: Free recall of 30-idea-unit science passages, one learning session, no feedback; effect absent on the immediate test.
agent_relevance: Background only: the agent has no forgetting, so the mechanism does not transfer. The lesson that a real check beats re-reading is already in G2/G3.

source: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Test-enhanced learning, Psychological Science, Exp 2
finding: Repeated testing (STTT) beat repeated study (SSSS) a week later even though students read the text only 3.4 times versus 14.2 times. Repeated study won on the 5-min test.
numbers: N=180, 30 per cell. 1 week: STTT 61%, SSST 56%, SSSS 40% (STTT vs SSSS d=1.26; SSST vs SSSS d=0.82). 5 min: SSSS 83% > SSST 78% > STTT 71%. Proportional forgetting over a week: SSSS 52%, SSST 28%, STTT 14%. STTT initial recall 20.9, 21.2, 21.1 of 30 units.
quote: restudying allowed students to reexperience 100% of the material but produced poor long-term retention
limits: Testing benefit is not just re-exposure. STTT vs SSST at one week only marginal (d=0.31). Initial test recall was about 70%, so retrieval was largely successful.
agent_relevance: Background only: the agent has no forgetting, so the mechanism does not transfer. The lesson that a real check beats re-reading is already in G2/G3.

source: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Test-enhanced learning, Exp 2 questionnaire (metacognition)
finding: Students who studied the most were most confident, and remembered the least. Students did not foresee the testing effect.
numbers: Predicted 1-week memory higher in SSSS than SSST (d=0.54) and STTT (d=0.61); actual 1-week recall ran the other way (40% vs 56% vs 61%).
limits: One university sample; ratings taken right after learning.
agent_relevance: Illusion of competence from fluency: a warning for any agent that trusts its own confidence after re-reading its own text (G1/G4).

source: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) The power of testing memory, Perspectives on Psychological Science (review)
finding: Historical review of about a century of testing studies: Abbott 1909, Gates 1917, Spitzer 1939, Tulving 1967, Hogan and Kintsch 1971 and later. Concludes the effect is secure but boundary conditions are open.
numbers: Gates 1917: recitation of 0 to 90% of study time, best near 60% for prose; first graders showed no effect. Bangert-Drowns 1991 meta-analysis of 35 classroom studies: 29 of 35 positive, mean d=0.23.
limits: Secondary account of old studies; Gates and Spitzer designs are loose by modern standards, but later replications (Forlano 1936; Sones and Stroud 1940) agree.
agent_relevance: Background only: the agent has no forgetting, so the mechanism does not transfer. The lesson that a real check beats re-reading is already in G2/G3.

source: Spitzer (1939) tests and retention in Iowa schools, as described in Roediger & Karpicke (2006) review
finding: Giant school study. A test soon after study nearly stopped forgetting. A first test given only on day 21 (forgetting already at floor) did not help later recall.
numbers: N=3,605 sixth graders in 91 schools; 600-word articles, 25 five-option multiple-choice items, tests spread over 63 days. Group tested right after study and a week later did much better at day 63 than Group 6 (first test on day 21).
limits: Read via the 2006 review, not the original. Multiple-choice, no feedback, so a first test must come while the item can still be recalled.
agent_relevance: Timing lesson: retrieval only helps if the item is still retrievable. Moot for a no-forgetting agent.

source: Tulving (1967) presentation and recall in free-recall learning, as described in Roediger & Karpicke (2006) review
finding: 36-word lists, 24 trials. STST, SSST and STTT gave similar learning curves, so a test trial can replace a study trial. This overturned the view that tests only measure learning.
numbers: Standard STST = 12 study and 12 test trials. SSST gave 18 study and 6 test; STTT gave 6 study and 18 test. Curves were similar.
limits: Read via review. Final recall was immediate, so long-term effect was not tested; Karpicke & Roediger 2007 added the 1-week test.
agent_relevance: Shows that a check step can do the work of a re-read step.

source: Karpicke & Roediger (2007) Repeated retrieval during learning is the key to long-term retention, JML, Exp 1
finding: Replicated Tulving with a 1-week final test. Repeated testing and standard alternation beat repeated study after a week. The best condition alternated study and test.
numbers: N=60. 1-week free recall (10 min): standard 68%, repeated test 64% (d=0.23 between them), repeated study about 57%. End of learning: standard 88%, repeated test 81%, repeated study 78%. Potentiating effect: tests raised new-item learning on the next study trial.
limits: Word lists, free recall, no feedback.
agent_relevance: Retrieval attempts make the next read more effective: test-then-read ordering.

source: Karpicke & Roediger (2007) Repeated retrieval ... JML, Exp 2 (dropout design)
finding: Dropping recalled items from further testing cut 1-week recall sharply. Dropping them from further study changed nothing. After first success, retrieval and not extra encoding did the work.
numbers: N=60. Items recalled once then dropped from testing: about 20% recall after a week. Items recalled 4 or 5 times: about 70%. Repeated retrieval beat dropout by more than 100%. STSNTN (all items recalled once then dropped) gave 21%; STST and STSNT about 36% (d=.41 and .47 above SSTT).
limits: Learning to a criterion of one recall is not enough. Word lists.
agent_relevance: Do not stop checking after the first pass if retention matters; an agent does not forget, so this is background.

source: Karpicke & Roediger (2008) The critical importance of retrieval for learning, Science
finding: Swahili-English pairs. After a pair was first recalled, repeated study had no effect a week later but repeated testing had a very large one. Predictions did not track this.
numbers: 40 pairs. Final recall about 80% in ST and SNT (repeated retrieval) vs 36% STN and 33% SNTN (dropped from testing); d=4.03 combined. Repeated study of recalled items: no gain. Trials: ST 320, SNT 236.8, STN 243.0, SNTN 154.8. Predictions about 50% in every condition (20.3 to 22.0 of 40).
limits: One lab, one paradigm; score ranges did not overlap (10-60% vs 63-95%). Effect size is unusually large.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that retrieval itself, not exposure, drives long-term gain.

source: Karpicke & Blunt (2011) Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping, Science
finding: Retrieval practice (study, then free recall twice) beat concept mapping from the text, on verbatim and inference questions, and even when the final test was a concept map. Students predicted the opposite.
numbers: Exp 1: N=80. Final test mean 0.67 retrieval vs 0.45 mapping (d=1.50, F(1,38)=21.63), about a 50% gain. Initial maps vs recall units equal (0.78 vs 0.81). Exp 2 replication: d=1.07 and 1.01 for short-answer and map final tests.
limits: Science texts; 1-week delay; mapping done with the text in view (elaborative study).
agent_relevance: Free recall plus restudy beats elaboration even on inference items. Supports retrieval-specific mechanisms.

source: Karpicke (2009) Metacognitive control and strategy selection, JEP General
finding: Given control, students dropped items after one correct recall. Self-chosen practice gave much worse retention than assigned retrieval practice.
numbers: Exp 1 N=30; test condition about .78 final recall. Exp 2 N=42: chosen strategies drop .60, test .25, study .15. Final recall overall .46. By item strategy: test .72, study .47, drop .35. Judgments of learning after a correct recall averaged .76.
limits: The .46 vs .78 comparison is across experiments. Students chose by retrieval fluency.
agent_relevance: Warning against letting the model decide when it has 'learned' something; supports program-controlled loops (section 1 of SCHEMA).

source: Karpicke & Roediger (2007) Expanding retrieval practice, JEPLMC, Exp 2 (feedback not given in Exp 1)
finding: Expanding schedule helped on a 10-min test (replicating Landauer and Bjork) but equal spacing was better after 2 days. Repeated tests beat a single test more at a delay.
numbers: N=48 (24 per retention group). Repeated vs single test: 2 days 39% vs 26% (d=0.75); 10 min 66% vs 61% (d=0.21). Massed retests gave near 98% recall during learning but the worst retention (about 20% at 2 days with and without feedback). Expanding vs equal recall during learning 77% vs 73%.
limits: Vocabulary pairs; short retention intervals.
agent_relevance: Spacing of checks matters more than a clever ordering.

source: Karpicke & Roediger (2007) Expanding retrieval practice, Exp 3 (delay of first test)
finding: Delaying the first test improved long-term retention whether later tests expanded or were equally spaced. Delay, which makes retrieval harder, is the active ingredient, not expansion.
numbers: Immediate vs delayed first test: 52% vs 44% (d=0.35); first-test recall fell with spacing (79% vs 73%, d=0.36). Feedback after a single delayed test gave 36% vs 19% for seven massed trials (d=0.66).
limits: Word pairs, small samples.
agent_relevance: Harder retrieval beats easy retrieval while success stays fairly high.

source: Latimier et al. (2021) meta-analysis of spaced retrieval, as reported in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Spaced retrieval strongly beats massed retrieval, but expanding schedules are no better than equal spacing.
numbers: Spaced vs massed g=0.74 (39 effect sizes). Expanding vs equal g=0.03 (54 effect sizes).
limits: Original meta-analysis not opened; numbers copied from the 2025 chapter.
agent_relevance: Do not build elaborate retrieval schedules; keep it simple.

source: Rowland (2014) testing vs restudy meta-analysis, as reported in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Overall testing effect over restudy is moderate and reliable. Larger at longer delay and larger when initial retrieval success is high.
numbers: 159 effect sizes: g=0.50 versus restudy; 81% of comparisons favour retrieval practice. Retention over 1 day g=0.69 vs under 1 day g=0.41. Effects more robust once initial retrieval success exceeds 75%.
limits: Original paper not opened; figures from the 2025 chapter, which says Adesope 2017, Agarwal 2021 and Yang 2021 reach similar conclusions.
agent_relevance: Gives the base rate: a medium effect that grows with delay.

source: Yang et al. (2021, 2023) classroom quizzing meta-analyses, as reported in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Classroom quizzing improves learning (Yang 2021) and lowers test anxiety (Yang 2023).
numbers: Test anxiety effect g=-0.52 across 25 effect sizes (Yang 2023). The 2021 learning effect size is not quoted in the chapter text I read.
limits: Original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Bjork & Bjork (1992) new theory of disuse, as described in Karpicke (2025) and Roediger & Karpicke (2006)
finding: Two strengths per memory: storage strength (lasting) and retrieval strength (momentary access). Retrieving an item with low retrieval strength gives a bigger rise in storage strength. Easy retrieval adds little.
numbers: Qualitative theory; no parameter values in the sources I read. Karpicke calls it a redescription of the effect rather than an explanation of mechanism.
limits: Read via two secondary accounts, not the 1992 chapter itself.
agent_relevance: Source of the desirable-difficulty idea; links to subfield 04.

source: Kornell, Bjork & Garcia (2011) bifurcation model, as described in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Testing splits items into recalled (strongly boosted) and not recalled (not boosted); restudy gives every item a modest boost. Same forgetting rate. This produces the crossover: restudy wins early, test wins late.
numbers: Verbal model; no fitted numbers in the source I read.
limits: Read via Karpicke 2025; original not opened. Related: Halamish and Bjork (2011).
agent_relevance: A small formal model that explains the immediate-versus-delayed reversal.

source: Lehman & Karpicke (2016) Elaborative retrieval: do semantic mediators improve memory?, JEPLMC
finding: Elaborative retrieval says searching memory brings up semantic mediators that get stored with the target. Measured mediator activation was not higher after retrieval than after restudy, and was unrelated or negatively related to later recall.
numbers: Exp 1a and 1b with 40 and 43 subjects (lexical-decision priming); initial recall about 86% correct. Mediator activation not higher on retrieve trials; unrelated or negatively related to cued recall.
limits: Word-pair materials only; Hausman and Rhodes (2018) found modest activation after retrieval, per Karpicke 2025.
agent_relevance: Evidence against an 'elaboration' explanation: the effect is not just thinking more about the item.

source: Carpenter (2009) weak versus strong associates, as described in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Weakly associated cues (basket-bread) gave a larger retrieval practice effect than strong cues (toast-bread), taken as support for elaborative retrieval.
numbers: No numbers quoted in the chapter.
limits: Read via Karpicke 2025; criticised for scope (word pairs only) and by later mediator tests.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Karpicke & Smith (2012) Separate mnemonic effects of retrieval practice and elaborative encoding, JML
finding: Repeated retrieval beat repeated study even when study used imagery keywords or verbal elaboration. Elaboration helped before first correct recall but gave nothing after it.
numbers: Exp 1: retrieval .73, repeated study .52, drop .37 (study vs drop F(1,58)=7.66). Exp 2: retrieval .67 > study (F(1,58)=8.55). Exp 3: retrieval .62 vs drop .36 (F(1,38)=43.77), vs study .45, vs elaboration .48 (F(1,38)=6.76). Exp 4 identical pairs (castle-castle): effect remained. Once recalled, next-trial recall p=.93.
limits: Word pairs; 40 to 60 subjects per experiment.
agent_relevance: Separates retrieval from elaboration; supports the episodic-context view.

source: Karpicke, Lehman & Aue (2014) episodic context account, as described in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Four assumptions: items are stored with temporal context; retrieval tries to reinstate that context; a successful retrieval updates the item's context with the test context; later retrieval uses the updated context. Built on SAM and the temporal context model.
numbers: Qualitative; explains why recall beats recognition and why spacing helps. Karpicke lists five criteria a theory should meet.
limits: Read via Karpicke 2025 only; original not opened.
agent_relevance: SAM and TCM could in principle be simulated; not needed for the agent.

source: Grimaldi & Karpicke (2012) When and why do retrieval attempts enhance subsequent encoding?, Memory & Cognition
finding: Failed retrieval attempts before study (pretesting) help when the pair is semantically related but not when unrelated. A forced wrong guess can hurt. A short delay between attempt and study removes the benefit.
numbers: Exp 1: related pairs pretest .73 vs no pretest .56; unrelated .24 vs .24. Exp 2: instructed guess .68 vs .57 (d=0.58); constrained retrieval (tide-wa__) .39 vs .57. Exp 3: .70 vs .56 (d=1.08) when immediate; none after a delay (.55 vs .56).
limits: Word pairs.
agent_relevance: Productive failure link (subfield 06): a wrong attempt helps only if cues are related.

source: Butler, Karpicke & Roediger (2008) Correcting a metacognitive error: feedback and low-confidence correct responses, JEPLMC
finding: Initial multiple-choice testing beat no testing and feedback added more. Feedback helped even correct answers when confidence was low, about doubling their retention.
numbers: Exp 1 N=30: final cued recall test+feedback .87, test only .41 (d=1.77), no test .24. Initially incorrect corrected .82 with feedback vs .03 without (d=6.08). Low-confidence correct kept .85 vs .40. Exp 2 (N=30, 2-day delay): feedback .83 vs .47; incorrect corrected .73 vs .09; correct kept .93 vs .78.
limits: General knowledge facts, multiple choice with confidence ratings.
agent_relevance: Feedback needs a source of truth; direct support for G2 (revise from real output).

source: Test format: Duchastel & Nungester (1982), Glover (1989), Kang et al. (2007), as described in Roediger & Karpicke (2006) review
finding: In 2006 the review said production tests (short answer, free recall) seemed to give bigger effects than multiple choice. Kang et al. (then in press): initial short-answer test with feedback gave best retention on both final formats. Duchastel and Nungester: effect at 2 weeks and 5 months for both formats.
numbers: No numbers for Kang et al. in the review text.
limits: Read via the 2006 review; the Kang paper itself was not opened. Later challenged (see Smith & Karpicke 2014).
agent_relevance: Format claim is not settled; retrieval success seems to matter more.

source: Smith & Karpicke (2014) Retrieval practice with short-answer, multiple-choice and hybrid tests, Memory
finding: Four experiments tried to reproduce the short-answer advantage. Short-answer and hybrid questions gave little or no benefit over multiple choice in three of four experiments. Only when short-answer success was raised (Exp 4) did the advantage appear.
numbers: N=372 across four experiments. Pooled short-answer vs multiple-choice d=0.07 (per Karpicke 2025). Exp 3 inference final test: MC better than SA, F(1,46)=3.97, partial eta2=.08. Exp 4: initial MC-vs-SA success gap narrowed to 13% from 42% and 32% in Exp 1 and 2.
limits: Educational texts, 1-week delay, feedback after retrieval; table layout garbled in the PDF text so cell values are not quoted.
agent_relevance: A failed replication of a founding claim in this series; retrieval success matters more than format.

source: Roediger & Marsh (2005); Butler et al. (2006); Marsh et al. (2009) negative effects of multiple choice, as described in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Picking a wrong option can plant false knowledge: students later produce the lures. More options help when initial success is high and hurt when it is low. Feedback largely removes the harm.
numbers: Marsh 2009: SAT II items; 5 min later short-answer final test; MC beat no test but lure intrusions rose. No figures quoted in the chapter.
limits: Read via Karpicke 2025; original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Wrong self-generated answers can stick; supports G2 and G3 (check against truth before keeping).

source: Karpicke & Grimaldi (2012) Retrieval-based learning: a perspective for enhancing meaningful learning, Educational Psychology Review
finding: Argues retrieval is the key process in learning and that students lack awareness of this. Describes classroom quizzing and a computer program that guides retrieval practice.
numbers: No new data; summary of Karpicke and Blunt 2011 and related work.
limits: Read abstract and framing only.
agent_relevance: Background.

source: Roediger & Karpicke (2018) Reflections on the resurgence of interest in the testing effect, Perspectives
finding: The 2006 article is in effect a conceptual replication of a century of findings. Authors say it has been widely replicated, directly and conceptually, with boundary conditions such as the immediate test. A classroom demonstration (Einstein, Mullet & Harrison 2012) reproduced it easily.
numbers: Citations by 2018 by the authors' count: the 2006 Psych Science article 1,589, the review 1,340.
limits: Written by the original investigators, so self-assessment.
agent_relevance: Context only.

source: Hanawalt (1937) repeated recall of figures, as described in Karpicke (2025)
finding: Subjects who recalled drawings once at different delays showed normal forgetting. Subjects who recalled repeatedly at each interval showed little or no forgetting over two months.
numbers: Intervals: immediate, 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 2 months. Values shown only in a figure.
limits: Read via Karpicke 2025.
agent_relevance: Repeated retrieval flattens the forgetting curve; for an agent with no forgetting this is moot.

source: Karpicke (2025) 4.21 Retrieval-based learning, Elsevier reference chapter (update of Karpicke 2017)
finding: Four theories: transfer-appropriate processing, strength and retrieval effort, elaborative retrieval, episodic context. The first two are heuristics, the third has failed tests. Working memory mostly does not moderate the effect. A text search of the chapter for language model, LLM and machine found nothing.
numbers: Working memory: most studies find no relation; a few find low-WM learners benefit more (Agarwal 2017; Yang 2020), one the opposite (Tse & Pu 2012).
limits: Single-author review by a founder of the area.
agent_relevance: No LLM link in the founding literature; AI work belongs to other angles.
